table.caption: Jobs the shop could print on its one press this Saturday, and what each is worth to the shop after materials (invented data for practice)

scarcity-s2.title: Juniper Ridge Bike Co. starts up
scarcity-s2.text: Ana Ruiz quits her job and puts her savings into a bike repair company, Juniper Ridge Bike Co. She rents a lot beside a river and uses its water to wash bikes. She hires two mechanics, buys wrenches, a repair stand and a delivery van, and spends her evenings deciding which repairs to offer and what to charge. (An invented company.)

items.q: What does scarcity mean in economics?
options: A good has run out in stores
People with low incomes face it, but others do not
Resources are limited while wants are unlimited
Prices are higher than people would like

why.correct: Scarcity is the gap between limited resources and unlimited wants. It is always present, not just when shelves are empty.
options: A store running out is a stock-out at one moment; scarcity never goes away.
Rich people, firms and governments face scarcity too, at least of time.
Right: limited resources, unlimited wants.
High prices can follow from scarcity, but they are not what it means.

items.q: A billionaire has more money than she could ever spend. Does she face scarcity?
options: Yes: her time is still limited
No: with enough money nothing is scarce
No: scarcity is a problem that firms face, not people
Yes, but just in years when prices are rising

why.correct: Money does not create more hours in a day. Every choice of how to spend her time still gives something up.
options: Right: time is scarce for everyone.
Money cannot buy more hours, so some choices still give things up.
Households and governments face scarcity too.
Scarcity does not depend on the price level.

items.q: Which of these is capital, as a factor of production?
options: Cash in the bakery's bank account
The baker's skill at decorating cakes
The wheat grown on a farm
An oven in a bakery

why.correct: Capital means goods made to produce other goods: tools, machines and buildings. An oven qualifies.
options: Money buys capital but is not itself a factor of production.
Effort and skill are labor.
Crops and other natural resources fall under land.
Right: a machine used to make bread.

items.q: Why is a well-known recipe less scarce than the flour used to bake it?
options: A recipe takes no time or effort to invent at first
Many can use it at once without using it up
Flour is a form of capital
Recipes are produced by the government

why.correct: Using flour uses it up, but one baker following a recipe does not stop another from following it too. Knowledge like this is not scarce in the usual way.
options: Inventing a recipe takes time and effort; what matters is that using it does not use it up.
Right: shared use does not use it up.
Flour is a raw material from land, not capital, and that is not the reason.
Recipes come from many people, and who made one does not matter here.

items.q: A free concert is held on a weeknight. For a student who would otherwise work a \$50 shift, what is the opportunity cost of going?
options: Zero, because the ticket is free
The \$50 shift she gives up
The price other people pay for concerts
The cost of the band's equipment

why.correct: The ticket price is zero, but going means giving up her next-best use of the evening: a shift worth \$50.
options: A free ticket still costs the time, and the time had another use.
Right: the next-best use of her time.
Other people's prices are not what she gives up.
The band's costs are not a choice she makes.

items.q: The shop chooses the wedding invitations. What is the opportunity cost of that choice, in dollars?

why.correct: The next-best job is the banners, worth \$650. Only one other job could have been printed, so the opportunity cost is $\max(650, 400) = 650$ dollars.

mistakes.why: That adds both jobs, but the press could print only one of them. The opportunity cost is the single next-best job.
That is the value of the job the shop chose. The opportunity cost is what it gave up: the next-best job.

items.q: Suppose the shop prints the store banners instead. What is the opportunity cost of that choice, in dollars?

why.correct: With the banners chosen, the next-best job is the wedding invitations, worth \$900.

mistakes.why: Only one other job could be printed. Take the best of the two, not their sum.

items.q: Why is printing the wedding invitations the best choice for the shop?
options: It has no opportunity cost
Its opportunity cost, \$1,050, is the lowest
It takes up less time on the press than either of the other jobs
Its \$900 value beats its \$650 opportunity cost

why.correct: A choice is worth making when its value is greater than the value of the next-best option it gives up: 900 > 650.
options: Every choice has an opportunity cost; here it is \$650.
\$1,050 adds both other jobs, which is not the opportunity cost.
Each job takes the press for the whole Saturday.
Right: 900 is more than 650.

items.q: A cafe raises its offer for the menus so they are worth \$1,000 to the shop. What happens to the opportunity cost of printing the wedding invitations?
options: It rises to \$1,000, more than the invitations are worth
It stays at \$650, because the banners still count
It falls to \$400, the value of the job left over
It rises to \$1,650

why.correct: Now the next-best job is the menus at \$1,000. The invitations, worth \$900, would give up more than they bring in.
options: Right: the menus become the next best.
The next-best option changed, so the opportunity cost changed.
The menus are now the most valuable alternative, not the least.
That adds two jobs; only the single next-best counts.

items.q: Which factor of production are the wrenches, the repair stand and the delivery van?
options: Land
Labor
Capital
Entrepreneurship

why.correct: Tools, machines and vehicles made to produce other goods and services are capital.
options: Land means natural resources such as the lot and the river water.
Labor is the mechanics' effort.
Right: tools and machines are capital.
Entrepreneurship is Ana's organizing and risk taking.

items.q: Which factor of production is the river water Ana uses to wash bikes?
options: Capital
Labor
Entrepreneurship
Land

why.correct: In economics, land means every natural resource: soil, water, minerals and the ground itself.
options: Capital is made by people; river water is not.
Water is not human effort.
Water is not the act of organizing a business.
Right: a natural resource.

items.q: Which factor of production does Ana supply by quitting her job, risking her savings and deciding what to offer and charge?
options: Labor
Capital
Entrepreneurship
Land

why.correct: Organizing the other factors and bearing the risk of the business is entrepreneurship.
options: Labor is the mechanics' repair work; Ana's role here is organizing and risk.
Her savings buy capital, but risking them and running the business is entrepreneurship.
Right: organizing and taking the risk.
Land is natural resources.

items.q: What is the opportunity cost of Ana starting the company?
options: Zero, because she owns the company
Her next-best option, such as her old job's pay
The rent on the lot and nothing else
Everything she could have done with the money and time, added up

why.correct: Starting the company meant giving up her next-best alternative, most likely her old job and what it paid.
options: Owning a business does not erase what she gave up to start it.
Right: her next-best alternative.
Rent is a payment she makes, but the opportunity cost of the choice is her best alternative.
Only the next-best alternative counts, not every possibility.

items.q: A city spends \$2 million on a new park instead of fixing roads. Which idea does this show?
options: A trade-off: the park money cannot also fix roads
Scarcity does not apply to governments
The park has no opportunity cost because it is public
The roads will be fixed for free

why.correct: Governments face scarcity too. Using money for one project means it is not available for another.
options: Right: one use gives up the other.
Governments have limited budgets, so they face scarcity.
Public projects still give up other uses of the money.
Fixing roads takes resources that now went to the park.

items.q: A pizzeria uses each of these. Which are labor? Select all that apply.
options: The cooks who make the pizzas
The drivers who deliver them
The pizza ovens
The tomatoes from a nearby farm

why.correct: Labor is human effort used in production: cooking and delivering both count.
options: Right: the cooks' effort is labor.
Right: the drivers' effort is labor.
Ovens are capital.
Farm produce comes from land, a natural resource.

items.q: A student says, "My opportunity cost of studying tonight is the money I spent on my textbook." What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing: past spending is the opportunity cost
Studying has no opportunity cost
The textbook money is gone either way; the cost is tonight's next-best use
The opportunity cost is the price of a brand-new copy of the textbook

why.correct: Opportunity cost looks forward: what you give up by choosing this over your next-best option now. Money already spent is not given up by tonight's choice.
options: Money spent in the past is not given up by a choice made now.
Every use of time gives up some other use.
Right: it is the next-best use of the evening.
Buying a new book is not what tonight's choice gives up.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the opportunity cost of a choice in order.
options: List the options you could choose
Pick the option you choose
Find the best of the options left over
Its value is the opportunity cost

why.correct: List the choices, set aside the one you take, and the best remaining one is what you give up.
